flashcards.q: Why does every Postgres UPDATE leave a dead tuple, and what reclaims it?
flashcards.a: Postgres never overwrites a row in place - UPDATE marks the old tuple's xmax and inserts a new version. The old version becomes a dead tuple, reclaimed only by VACUUM/autovacuum once no active transaction's snapshot needs it.

flashcards.q: Does plain VACUUM shrink the table file on disk?
flashcards.a: No - it reclaims dead-tuple space for reuse within the existing file. Only VACUUM FULL (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, full rewrite) or pg_repack (online) actually shrink the file.

flashcards.q: Autovacuum trigger formula and why the default is dangerous on huge tables?
flashcards.a: dead_tuples > autovacuum_vacuum_threshold(50) + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor(0.2) x total_rows. On a 500M-row table, 20% = 100M dead tuples before autovacuum even runs - too late for high-churn tables, requiring per-table scale_factor overrides.

flashcards.q: What is transaction ID wraparound and why does it force a full outage?
flashcards.a: 32-bit XIDs wrap every ~4B transactions with an unambiguous comparison window of ~2B either direction. Old unfrozen tuples risk appearing invisible/ambiguous post-wrap (data corruption risk), so Postgres hard-stops new writes as the oldest unfrozen XID approaches the limit - a deliberate safety valve, not a bug.

flashcards.q: What number do you alert on to prevent XID wraparound outages?
flashcards.a: age(datfrozenxid) per database via pg_database - alert well before the ~2 billion hard limit (start around 1 billion). Fully preventable; weeks of log warnings precede any real incident.

flashcards.q: What is a HOT update and what disqualifies a row from it?
flashcards.a: Heap-Only Tuple update: new version written on the SAME page with a forwarding pointer, zero index writes. Requires no indexed column changed AND the new tuple fits on the same page. Breaking either condition forces a full update touching ALL indexes on the table.

flashcards.q: What is TOAST and what's its practical performance implication?
flashcards.a: Values over ~2KB are compressed/moved out of the 8KB page into a side table (pg_toast), chunked, with a pointer left in the row. Detoast cost is paid per row per TOASTed column actually accessed - SELECT * on wide JSONB tables costs more than selecting only needed columns.

flashcards.q: Explain the FIFO lock queue trap with ALTER TABLE.
flashcards.a: A long-running SELECT holds ACCESS SHARE; a queued ALTER TABLE (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) waits for it; every SUBSEQUENT SELECT also queues behind the ALTER TABLE, even though SELECT-SELECT would normally be compatible - because Postgres's lock queue is FIFO.

flashcards.q: Why is raising max_connections alone not the fix for connection exhaustion?
flashcards.a: Each Postgres connection is a full OS process consuming several MB plus setup cost - practical ceiling is hundreds to low thousands, not tens of thousands. PgBouncer (transaction pooling) multiplexes many clients onto fewer backend connections instead.

flashcards.q: What does PgBouncer's transaction pooling mode break in an application?
flashcards.a: Session-level state that doesn't persist across a shared physical connection: prepared statements, session-level SET variables, and advisory locks held outside an explicit transaction.

flashcards.q: What did Postgres 18 add, and why?
flashcards.a: Asynchronous I/O (AIO) subsystem (up to 3x read improvement), skip scan for multicolumn B-tree indexes, and uuidv7() - a time-ordered UUID built-in fixing the index bloat/cache-locality problem caused by random UUIDv4 primary keys.

flashcards.q: Why does a random UUIDv4 primary key cause worse index bloat than a sequential ID, and what's the uuidv7 tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Random values scatter inserts uniformly across the B-Tree's key range, causing page splits and cache misses instead of appending near the end. uuidv7() embeds a timestamp for monotonic ordering, but this leaks approximate creation time if the ID is exposed externally.

flashcards.q: pgvector: IVFFlat vs HNSW, and when do you still need a dedicated vector database?
flashcards.a: IVFFlat needs a training step, faster build, worse recall/latency. HNSW needs no training, current default recommendation. Choose a dedicated vector DB over pgvector at hundreds of millions of vectors with strict recall/latency SLAs.

flashcards.q: Why sort pg_stat_statements by total_exec_time rather than mean_exec_time?
flashcards.a: A query called 100,000 times at 5ms averages costs far more aggregate database time (500s) than one slow query called once - total_exec_time finds the most actionable target for reducing overall DB load; mean/max_exec_time is for tail-latency/SLO hunting instead.

flashcards.q: What does logical replication depend on, and what's the common production incident related to it?
flashcards.a: A replication slot, which retains WAL segments until its consumer confirms processing them. A disconnected/stuck consumer (e.g. Debezium) is one of the most common causes of WAL directory disk exhaustion in production Postgres.
